paragraphs: Learning functions is central to many scientific and engineering problems, but increasingly complex machine learning models can be expensive to train and run. This paper explores a different route: using a dynamical system as the computing mechanism. Its proposed system, EADS, addresses two weaknesses the authors identify in existing approaches: limited ability to represent complicated functions and inefficient training.

EADS combines a hierarchical architecture with heterogeneous dynamics, meaning its components can exhibit different kinds of behavior. Inspired by biological systems, this combination expands the range of functions the system can represent. The authors also introduce on-device training that uses the system’s own electrical signals to update its parameters, connecting adaptation directly to its physical operation.

Experiments across several domains report higher accuracy than existing work and orders-of-magnitude speedups over traditional neural networks running on GPUs, for both training and inference. These findings support the proposed combination of expressive dynamics and local adaptation as a route to efficient function learning in the evaluated settings.
icml-2025-an-expressive-and-self-adaptiv.tldr: EADS combines hierarchical dynamics with electrical-signal-based training to learn functions with reported accuracy gains and large training and inference speedups.

paragraphs: Pruning a trained language model requires deciding which weights can be removed with the least damage. The scoring rule used for that decision is therefore crucial. This paper argues that simple combinations of weight values and activations can give misleading priorities because weight magnitudes differ across channels and unusually large activations can dominate the scores.

BaWA adjusts both sources of imbalance. Magnitude normalization makes weights from different channels more comparable, while outlier regularization reduces the influence of extreme activation values. Together, these changes aim to make removal decisions better reflect useful model structure. An automatic optimization framework selects the normalization and regularization hyperparameters, making the balancing procedure part of the method rather than leaving it entirely to manual tuning.

The authors report state-of-the-art pruning results. For Mistral-7B with 2:4 sparsity, BaWA improves on Wanda by lowering perplexity by 2.49 and raising average downstream task accuracy by 3.08%. This example illustrates how improving the pruning metric can preserve more capability under a specified sparsity pattern.
icml-2025-bawa-automatic-optimizing-prun.tldr: BaWA improves language-model pruning by normalizing weight magnitudes, limiting activation outliers, and automatically tuning these adjustments.

paragraphs: Diffusion models can produce strong super-resolution results, but their memory and computation demands complicate deployment on constrained devices. BiMaCoSR combines two compression strategies: representing model weights with one bit and distilling a process with multiple diffusion steps into a single step. The challenge is preserving image-generation capability when these aggressive reductions are applied together.

The method adds two auxiliary branches that retain full-precision information. A sparse matrix branch absorbs extreme values and supplies a high-rank output carrying richer information. A low-rank matrix branch, inspired by LoRA and initialized from leading singular-value decomposition components, supplies a compact representation. These branches provide complementary information to counter the model collapse that binarization can cause, with overhead the authors describe as negligible.

Experiments report better performance than existing state-of-the-art binarization methods and competitive results against a full-precision one-step model. Relative to its full-precision counterpart, BiMaCoSR achieves 23.8-fold compression and a 27.4-fold speedup. The findings demonstrate a substantial efficiency gain while retaining competitive super-resolution performance in the reported comparisons.
icml-2025-bimacosr-binary-one-step-diffu.tldr: BiMaCoSR combines one-bit compression and one-step diffusion with two full-precision auxiliary branches to accelerate super-resolution while preserving competitive quality.

paragraphs: A forecasting model that performs well overall may still be a poor choice for particular inputs. Through inspection of individual test samples, this paper finds that different models excel in different cases, with no single model consistently winning. TimeFuse uses this observation to make model combination depend on the time series being forecast.

The framework describes each input through meta-features and feeds them to a learned fusion component. That component predicts how much weight to give each forecasting model for the current sample. Because the underlying models can differ, the framework can combine distinct forecasting strengths. Its fusion component can also train jointly on samples from several datasets, exposing it to a wider variety of temporal patterns.

Experiments cover both short-term and long-term forecasting and report improvements over state-of-the-art individual models in nearly all evaluated cases. The authors also describe generalization to inputs from previously unseen datasets. These findings support adapting the combination to each input, while the near-universal improvement claim remains an empirical result rather than a guarantee.
icml-2025-breaking-silos-adaptive-model-.tldr: TimeFuse learns input-specific weights for combining forecasting models, producing improvements over individual models in nearly all reported evaluations.

paragraphs: A learning rule intended to help explain the brain should do more than solve a behavioral task: its trained network should also resemble recorded neural activity. This paper examines that second requirement, which has received less attention than task performance. It compares e-prop, a biologically plausible rule based on truncated gradients, with backpropagation through time.

Using neuroscience datasets and comparison methods including Procrustes analysis, the authors find that e-prop can achieve neural similarity comparable to backpropagation through time when task accuracy is matched. That condition matters: the comparison concerns networks performing at comparable levels. The result establishes that at least one biologically plausible learning rule can meet this neural-similarity benchmark in the studied settings.

The study also finds that architecture and initial conditions can influence neural similarity more strongly than the learning rule. Networks trained with the two approaches exhibit similar dynamical properties at comparable accuracies. Together, these findings support the potential of biologically plausible rules while showing why neural similarity must be interpreted alongside network design and task performance.
icml-2025-can-biologically-plausible-tem.tldr: At matched task accuracy, e-prop can match backpropagation through time in similarity to neural recordings, with architecture and initialization sometimes mattering more.

paragraphs: Multi-view clustering groups data using complementary information from several sources. Applying it across distributed participants creates additional challenges: communication can be costly, shared representations can expose sensitive information, and some participants or examples may lack certain views. EFIMVC is designed to address these concerns together within a federated clustering framework.

The method uses localized optimization to reduce communication, accompanied by a theoretical convergence result. For the information that must be exchanged, it uses both view-specific and shared anchor graphs. This choice avoids sending sensitive embeddings and provides a way to communicate structure relevant to clustering. The framework also accommodates missing views, so its operation does not require every source of information to be present.

Benchmark experiments report advantages in clustering accuracy, communication efficiency, and privacy preservation. The contribution is the combination of these properties within one approach: reducing exchanges while retaining useful information across views and supporting incomplete data. Its privacy benefit is tied to avoiding embedding transmission; the abstract does not frame that design choice as an absolute guarantee against disclosure.
icml-2025-efficient-federated-incomplete.tldr: EFIMVC combines local optimization and anchor-graph communication to improve federated clustering efficiency, privacy preservation, and handling of missing views.

paragraphs: Autoregressive mesh generators represent a mesh as a sequence and predict its coordinates progressively. The tokenizer determines how that geometry becomes a sequence, making its representation an important part of the generation pipeline. This paper addresses the difficulty of evaluating different mesh tokenizers efficiently, without first training a model for each candidate.

The authors introduce Per-Token-Mesh-Entropy, or PTME, as a theoretical metric that can evaluate existing tokenizers without training. Building on this metric, they propose coordinate merging: a technique that rearranges and combines frequently occurring coordinate patterns. It is designed to plug into existing tokenizers and increase their compression ratios, improving how compactly mesh information is represented.

Experiments with MeshXL, MeshAnything V2, and Edgerunner validate the proposed method across several tokenization approaches. The contribution therefore has two linked parts: a way to assess tokenizers and a practical modification informed by that assessment. The authors position both as tools for improving existing representations and guiding future mesh-generation development, rather than presenting that future impact as established.
icml-2025-freemesh-boosting-mesh-generat.tldr: FreeMesh introduces a training-free metric for mesh tokenizers and a coordinate-merging technique that improves their compression ratios.

paragraphs: Shuffling gradient methods optimize an objective built from a finite collection of component functions, together with regularization. They process those functions individually in an order specified by a permutation. Although these methods are straightforward to implement and effective in practice, understanding the quality of their final update has been harder, particularly when the objective is nonsmooth.

This paper improves the theoretical analysis of that final update, known as the last iterate, for nonsmooth convex and strongly convex problems. It shows that both Random Reshuffle and Single Shuffle have convergence guarantees faster than those of proximal gradient descent. Earlier bounds for these nonsmooth settings had only matched proximal gradient descent, so the new analysis exposes a provable benefit from random ordering.

The results also yield a nearly optimal guarantee for averaging a suffix of the updates under Random Reshuffle in the general convex setting. That guarantee matches the cited lower bound to the stated degree. These are convergence-rate results: they sharpen what can be established about optimization progress, rather than reporting measured runtime improvements.
icml-2025-improved-last-iterate-converge.tldr: The paper proves improved last-iterate convergence rates for randomized shuffling methods on nonsmooth convex objectives, exceeding proximal gradient descent guarantees.

paragraphs: Making language-model activations sparse can reduce computation and memory transfers during inference. Existing approaches may require costly recovery training or produce varying sparsity through magnitude-based decisions, making speed gains unstable. LaRoSA aims to obtain predictable sparsity and practical acceleration without an additional training stage.

Its central step is an orthogonal rotation of the input activations at each layer. This changes their representation into a form better suited to sparsification. A Top-K selection procedure then operates on the rotated activations, giving consistent sparsity across the model. The approach therefore connects the representation used for sparsification with explicit control over how much activity is retained.

Across different language-model types and sizes, the authors report acceleration with small performance losses. For LLaMA2-7B at 40% sparsity, they report a 0.17 perplexity gap and a 1.30-fold wall-clock speedup. The zero-shot accuracy gap from the dense model is 0.54%, with improvements over TEAL and CATS of 1.77% and 17.14%, respectively. These results demonstrate a measured efficiency-quality tradeoff at the reported setting.
icml-2025-la-rosa-enhancing-llm-efficien.tldr: LaRoSA rotates activations before Top-K sparsification to deliver consistent language-model sparsity and measured inference speedups without additional training.

paragraphs: Linear Q-learning represents action values using a linear function rather than a separate entry for every situation. Its potential instability has been a longstanding concern. Building on a prior result establishing eventual almost-sure boundedness, this paper provides the first L2 convergence rate for its iterates toward a bounded set, giving a quantitative mean-square account of their behavior.

The analysis keeps the original linear Q-learning update unchanged. It does not require Bellman completeness or a behavior policy that is nearly optimal. It does require an epsilon-softmax behavior policy with an adaptive temperature. The bounded-set destination is essential to the claim: the result should not be read as convergence to the optimal action-value function.

The proof relies on a more general result for stochastic approximation with Markovian noise and rapidly changing transition functions. The authors also apply this tool to tabular Q-learning with an epsilon-softmax policy, establishing an L2 convergence rate through a new pseudo-contraction property of a weighted Bellman optimality operator. The contribution thus includes both a specific stability guarantee and an analytical tool.
icml-2025-linear-q-learning-does-not-div.tldr: Under an adaptive-temperature epsilon-softmax behavior policy, unchanged linear Q-learning has a provable L2 convergence rate to a bounded set.

paragraphs: The Segment Anything Model can segment unfamiliar images, but substantial changes in the target domain can degrade its performance. Adaptation methods often use a fixed teacher to supervise a student. This paper identifies a weakness in that arrangement: under severe distribution shifts, the designated teacher may not remain the more reliable network.

The proposed source-free framework uses two collaborating networks and reassesses their teacher and student roles at every training iteration. Reliability determines which network provides guidance. Three losses support this exchange: direct alignment transfers knowledge, reverse distillation encourages diversity, and a triplet relationship loss improves feature representations. The design combines learning from a stronger partner with maintaining useful differences between the networks.

Experiments across diverse target domains report state-of-the-art adaptation performance. The authors describe the framework as improving target-domain generalization while preserving pretrained knowledge. Its central contribution is making the direction of supervision responsive to changing network reliability, so collaboration does not depend on one network retaining a fixed advantage throughout adaptation.
icml-2025-mutual-learning-for-sam-adapta.tldr: Two SAM networks dynamically exchange teacher and student roles based on reliability, improving source-free adaptation across the evaluated target domains.

paragraphs: Learning physical systems can involve discovering an operator that maps one function to another from only a limited collection of examples. The paper frames this as a severely ill-posed inverse partial differential equation problem. Its proposed architecture, Neural Interpretable PDEs, builds on Nonlocal Attention Operators to improve both prediction and computational efficiency.

The architecture combines linear attention with a learnable kernel network operating as a channel-independent convolution in Fourier space. This arrangement handles spatial interactions without explicitly constructing and storing large collections of pairwise relationships. Instead, the Fourier transform carries much of the cost of representing those interactions, offering a more scalable route to learning the operator.

Across diverse benchmarks, the authors report that the architecture consistently outperforms Nonlocal Attention Operators and other baselines. The findings support the value of combining attention with Fourier-based computation for the evaluated physics-learning tasks. The concrete efficiency contribution is the removal of explicit large pairwise interaction storage and computation, alongside the reported predictive gains.
icml-2025-neural-interpretable-pdes-harm.tldr: Neural Interpretable PDEs combines linear attention and Fourier-space kernels to improve physical-system prediction while avoiding large explicit pairwise interactions.

paragraphs: Electronic health records support cohort studies, where patients sharing characteristics or diseases are examined over time. Useful modeling depends both on identifying meaningful patient groups and on understanding relationships within and between them. This paper argues that existing approaches struggle to form sufficiently detailed cohorts and to make effective use of the cohort information they contain.

NeuralCohort introduces a contextualization mechanism that divides patients into finer-grained cohorts. Its Biscale Cohort Learning Module then captures information at two levels: relationships among patients within a cohort and relationships across cohorts. These signals become part of the learned patient representations. The method is designed as a plug-in, allowing existing backbone models to incorporate cohort structure into their learning process.

Evaluations on real-world health-record datasets show consistent improvements across various backbone models, with a reported AUROC increase of up to 8.1%. That upper-end result describes predictive performance in the experiments. The broader finding is that explicitly modeling cohort context can improve existing representations rather than requiring a completely new backbone.
icml-2025-neuralcohort-cohort-aware-neur.tldr: NeuralCohort adds fine-grained patient grouping and within- and across-cohort learning to existing health-record models, improving their reported predictive performance.

paragraphs: Adversarial examples can transfer between neural networks because different models rely on some of the same important features. This paper examines why existing feature-level attacks still have limited transferability. Its theoretical finding is that repeated pixel-space perturbations in those attacks have an effect equivalent to a single feature-space step along the direction of feature importance.

P2FA changes the space in which the attack is optimized. It perturbs the features directly through multiple updates guided by their importance, then converts the altered features back into pixels to create the adversarial example. The intended advantage is that repeated updates can more effectively disrupt shared critical features, rather than producing only the equivalent of one feature-space perturbation.

The authors report superior transferability over state-of-the-art attacks across numerous experiments. These findings support their explanation that where perturbations are applied can matter as much as repeating them. The contribution links a theoretical diagnosis of an existing inefficiency to an attack procedure that directly targets the affected representation.
icml-2025-pixel2feature-attack-p2fa-reth.tldr: P2FA repeatedly perturbs important features directly before converting them back to pixels, improving adversarial transferability in the reported experiments.

paragraphs: Interactive 3D segmentation uses a person’s clicks to identify an object within a complex scene. A useful system must infer the rest of the object from limited guidance and indicate where its predictions may be unreliable. NPISeg3D addresses both needs through a probabilistic framework based on Neural Processes.

The model uses a hierarchy of latent variables: one level represents the scene, while another captures characteristics of individual objects. This lets sparse clicks be interpreted using both broader context and object-specific information. A probabilistic prototype modulator further adapts the representations associated with clicks using the object-level latent variables, supporting object-aware predictions and uncertainty estimation within the same framework.

Experiments on four 3D point-cloud datasets report better segmentation with fewer clicks, alongside reliable uncertainty estimates. The results support combining contextual inference and uncertainty modeling rather than treating user guidance only as a set of isolated labels. For interaction, the two benefits are complementary: fewer clicks can produce useful masks, and uncertainty can help users recognize regions that merit further attention.
icml-2025-probabilistic-interactive-3d-s.tldr: NPISeg3D uses scene- and object-level latent variables to improve 3D segmentation from sparse clicks while estimating prediction uncertainty.

paragraphs: Aligning language models with human expectations often depends on high-quality training data. Methods that generate extra responses can expand that data, but the quality of generated material changes as the model learns. This paper argues that treating generation and training as separate, static processes overlooks their dependence on each other and wastes useful information.

Progressively Label Enhancement, or PLE, makes training decisions responsive to the evolving generated data. The model produces responses to an original query and to carefully designed versions guided by principles. Reward scores assess those responses, and a dynamic threshold determines the appropriate training approach for them. This makes the treatment of generated examples change with their assessed quality.

Experiments show that PLE is effective compared with existing alignment methods. Its contribution is a feedback-aware organization of data generation and model training: generated responses are evaluated within an adapting process instead of being assigned a fixed role throughout learning. The reported findings support this dynamic use of generated data as a practical approach to alignment.
icml-2025-progressively-label-enhancemen.tldr: PLE adapts language-model alignment training using reward scores and a changing threshold for responses generated from original and principle-guided queries.

paragraphs: Time-series classification depends on recognizing how a signal evolves. Reservoir computing can extract temporal dynamics efficiently, but typical systems update through neighboring states and struggle to capture relationships over longer intervals. SARC addresses this weakness by using frequency information to expose repeating patterns that may be explicit or hidden in the signal.

The framework first identifies prominent frequencies. For each frequency, a Frequency-informed Reservoir Network captures both the sequential progression of the data and its cyclical behavior. SARC then combines the resulting dynamic features across frequencies. This provides several temporal scales for describing the same input, helping connect local evolution with patterns that recur over longer periods.

Experiments on public datasets report state-of-the-art classification performance while retaining high efficiency relative to existing methods. The findings support supplementing reservoir dynamics with spectral structure, rather than expecting adjacent-state recursion alone to capture every useful dependency. The method’s central contribution is a coordinated representation of sequential and cyclical behavior across the extracted frequencies.
icml-2025-spectral-aware-reservoir-compu.tldr: SARC combines frequency-informed reservoir networks to capture sequential and cyclical patterns, improving long-range time-series classification while retaining efficiency.

paragraphs: Prompt learning adapts a pretrained vision-language model by learning prompts with relatively few trainable parameters. Using several diverse prompts can describe visual concepts from different perspectives and improve downstream performance. However, learning that diversity can require substantial computation, creating an efficiency problem even within a parameter-efficient adaptation strategy.

Surrogate Prompt Learning changes what the framework generates. Instead of learning many text prompts, it uses a lightweight Surrogate Feature Generator to produce the corresponding prompted text features directly. Starting from a basic prompted feature, the generator receives different predefined conditional signals and produces diverse representations. This avoids the complex gradient computation associated with conventional diverse prompt learning.

Experiments across several benchmarks report effective surrogate features together with strong performance and efficiency. The result supports obtaining useful representational diversity through a smaller feature-generating component. The key distinction is between creating multiple prompts and creating the features those prompts are meant to supply: SurPL focuses computation on the latter while retaining the intended diversity.
icml-2025-surrogate-prompt-learning-towa.tldr: SurPL efficiently produces diverse prompted text features with a lightweight generator instead of learning many separate text prompts.

paragraphs: Models of spatial and temporal systems are often trained independently for each source, limiting the reuse of knowledge even across related tasks. SynEVO aims to make learning cumulative across domains. Inspired by neuroscience, the authors derive an increased information boundary from cross-domain collective learning and build a framework that shares and aggregates knowledge.

The framework first reorders groups of samples to imitate curriculum learning. It then combines an elastic common container with a task-independent extractor, supporting model growth while separating shared structure from task-specific characteristics. An adaptive dynamic coupler uses a new difference metric to decide whether a new sample group should enter the common container. This makes incorporation of new information an explicit part of model evolution.

Experiments report improvements in cross-domain generalization of up to 42%. That figure is the largest stated improvement, rather than a uniform gain across settings. The findings support selective knowledge sharing and evolving common representations as an approach to transfer, connecting the proposed collective-learning theory with a concrete adaptation mechanism.
icml-2025-synevo-a-neuro-inspired-spatio.tldr: SynEVO selectively incorporates knowledge across domains into an evolving spatiotemporal model, with reported generalization gains of up to 42%.

paragraphs: TabPFN predicts labels for tabular examples by using labeled training examples as context. Its strengths on small classification problems do not fully resolve challenges involving many features, larger datasets, or mismatch with a downstream task. This paper argues that adaptations often address either bias or variance while neglecting the other and increasing inference costs.

Beta combines encoder-based adaptation with bagging to address both. A lightweight encoder aligns downstream data more closely with the pretrained TabPFN, targeting bias. Increasing the number of lightweight encoders targets variance, while bootstrapped sampling further reduces sensitivity to data perturbations. These components are designed to improve adaptation while keeping inference computationally efficient.

On more than 200 benchmark classification datasets, Beta reportedly matches or exceeds state-of-the-art methods. The authors also report improved handling of high-dimensional inputs and scaling to larger datasets. The contribution is the coordinated treatment of task alignment and prediction variability, showing how several lightweight adaptation mechanisms can broaden the usefulness of an existing in-context tabular model.
icml-2025-tabpfn-unleashed-a-scalable-an.tldr: Beta combines lightweight encoders and bootstrapped sampling to improve TabPFN’s adaptation, stability, and scalability across tabular classification tasks.

paragraphs: Time series can change their statistical behavior over time, creating different problems at different forecasting scales. This paper argues that short-term non-stationarity can produce misleading relationships, while longer-term changes can reveal cointegration across variables. Removing or retaining non-stationarity everywhere therefore fails to distinguish these two roles.

TimeBridge divides input series into smaller patches and assigns distinct attention mechanisms to the two scales. Integrated Attention reduces short-term non-stationarity to capture stable dependencies within each variable. Cointegrated Attention retains non-stationarity to model long-term relationships across variables. The framework makes the treatment of changing statistics depend on the type of dependency it is trying to learn.

Experiments report consistently state-of-the-art results for both short-term and long-term forecasting, with particularly strong financial forecasting results on the CSI 500 and S&P 500 indices. These findings support the paper’s central design choice: local stabilization and preservation of long-term structure can work together. The reported financial results extend that empirical support to the two evaluated index settings.
icml-2025-timebridge-non-stationarity-ma.tldr: TimeBridge suppresses short-term non-stationarity while preserving long-term changes to model dependencies within and across time-series variables.

paragraphs: Real-world time series often change over time in ways that make forecasting difficult. A model needs to recognize the overall behavior of a signal while remaining sensitive to local details. TimeStacker is designed around this combination, addressing the difficulty existing models have in representing non-stationary signals.

Its central mechanism stacks observations to capture global signal features alongside finer local information. The framework also includes a frequency-based self-attention module to strengthen feature modeling. These components bring together multilevel observation and frequency information, giving the predictor complementary ways to represent a changing signal. The approach matters because broad structure and local variation both contribute to the forecasting problem described by the authors.

Experiments span real-world datasets from energy, finance, and weather. The authors report superior predictive accuracy together with fewer parameters and greater computational efficiency. The findings therefore concern both forecasting quality and model economy: in the evaluated settings, the proposed representation improves predictions without requiring a larger or more computationally demanding model.
icml-2025-timestacker-a-novel-framework-.tldr: TimeStacker combines global and local observations with frequency-based attention, reporting better forecasting accuracy with fewer parameters and higher efficiency.

paragraphs: Medical images vary across devices and collection centers, making it difficult for a model trained in one domain to generalize elsewhere. TinyMIG aims to transfer the generalization capabilities of vision foundation models into lightweight specialized models. Its training approach asks the smaller model to imitate both broad feature structure and fine-grained local information.

For global structure, Global Distribution Consistency Learning matches the foundation model’s prior feature distributions layer by layer. For local detail, Localized Representation Alignment encourages semantic agreement between the specialized model and the foundation model. The two mechanisms address different scales of representation, so transfer is not limited to matching only an overall distribution or only localized features.

Large-scale benchmark experiments report that TinyMIG significantly outperforms state-of-the-art models at extremely low computational cost. The findings support this combination of global and local guidance for single-domain generalization in the evaluated medical-imaging scenarios. The practical aim is to make a lightweight specialized model benefit from a foundation model’s broader representations during training.
icml-2025-tinymig-transferring-generaliz.tldr: TinyMIG transfers global feature distributions and local semantic details from vision foundation models to lightweight medical-imaging models for stronger single-domain generalization.

paragraphs: Visual prompting adapts a pretrained Vision Transformer by learning a small set of prompts. This paper argues that sharing the same prompts across all tokens ignores their different roles and can yield features that are hard to distinguish or biased. Token Coordinated Prompt Attention addresses this by tailoring prompt interactions to the tokens they serve.

The module first separates prompts for the CLS token, which aggregates global information, from prompts for image tokens, which extract local features. Each group interacts exclusively with its corresponding token type. Because individual image tokens represent different patches, a matching function then assigns coordinated prompts to particular tokens. This adds specificity both between token roles and among local image regions.

Experiments across several benchmarks report substantial improvements in feature diversity and discriminative power. The findings support a more selective use of a small prompt set: adaptation depends on matching prompts to distinct informational roles. As a plug-and-play module, TCPA is intended to add that coordination to visual prompting rather than require an entirely new pretrained backbone.
icml-2025-token-coordinated-prompt-atten.tldr: TCPA assigns prompts according to global and local token roles, improving the diversity and discriminative power of visual-prompting features.

paragraphs: Chain-of-thought prompting can improve language-model reasoning, but its benefits vary across tasks. This paper investigates whether token probability distributions can help predict when it will be useful. Its starting observation is preliminary: the monotonicity of those distributions may correlate with the performance gains from chain-of-thought reasoning.

The authors construct two indicators from token probabilities and combine instance-level signals with logistic regression. The resulting Dynamic CoT method chooses between generating a chain of thought and answering directly. They also extend the approach to closed-source models by transferring decision strategies learned from open-source models. The indicators thus become a mechanism for allocating extra reasoning selectively.

The reported indicators assess chain-of-thought effectiveness with 89.2% accuracy, while Dynamic CoT reduces token consumption by more than 35% and maintains high accuracy. These findings support the usefulness of the signals for selective deployment. They do not turn the preliminary correlation into a complete explanation of why chain-of-thought works; the contribution is both an investigative perspective and an empirically effective selection method.
icml-2025-token-signature-predicting-cha.tldr: Dynamic CoT uses token-probability indicators to choose when to reason step by step, cutting reported token use by over 35% while maintaining high accuracy.
